samples.summary: The `deviceSecret` salting the Yorkie client key is per-browser-profile, not per-account, so on the shared device this feature is designed for one signed-in user can derive every other user's per-document client key
samples.evidence:
`durableClientKey()` returns `wb:{deviceSecret}:{userId}:{docKey}` (durable-session.ts:96-98) and `deviceSecret()` reads a single `localStorage` key `wafflebase-durable-device` (line 110, 137-154) that is **not scoped to an account** — every user who signs in on that browser profile reads and writes the same value.

The module's own comment (lines 80-94) states the threat: Yorkie authorizes `ActivateClient`/`DeactivateClient` on token validity alone, so anybody holding any valid token who can *derive* a client key can activate or tear it down. I confirmed that authorization model in this repo: `packages/backend/src/document/yorkie-auth.controller.ts:69` defines `CLIENT_METHODS = new Set(['ActivateClient','DeactivateClient'])` and line 292-296 returns `ALLOW` for them with no document and no client-key ownership check; `docs/design/yorkie-auth-webhook.md:82` says the same ("No document. Validate token only").

Vector: attacker A signs in once on a shared/kiosk/borrowed browser profile and reads `localStorage['wafflebase-durable-device']`. From then on, from any machine, A computes `wb:{stolenSecret}:{B_userId}:{sheet-<docId>}` for any workspace peer B — `B_userId` is the sequential id every member list carries and `docId` sits in the URL, both public to a peer, exactly as the comment notes. Holding only A's own valid Yorkie token, A calls `DeactivateClient` (or activates the key first) against B's per-document client, stranding or taking over the durable session B's unsent work depends on.

Second, weaker vector on the same root cause: the "secret" is transmitted to the Yorkie server as part of the client key on every activate and stored in the client row, so it is not confidential against anything that can read a client listing, an admin view, or a server log that echoes a client key — and one leaked key yields the secret for the whole device, hence every user and document on it.

I could not verify Yorkie's server-side behaviour on a duplicate/foreign client key from this repo, so the exact consequence (DoS vs. takeover) is unconfirmed; the derivation itself and the permissive webhook decision are both traced in code.

samples.summary: An involuntarily ended session erases nothing at all, so full document snapshots plus change logs stay on a possibly shared device for up to 30 days; the `keepArchives` middle ground the store was built for has no caller
samples.evidence:
`fetchWithAuth`'s 401 arm passes `eraseLocalData: "none"` (api/auth.ts:277) and `logout()` therefore skips `eraseOfflineDataOnLogout()` entirely (api/auth.ts:134). Nothing else runs on an expired session: `retryPendingOfflineErase()` only fires on the *next* sign-in (offline-erase.ts:352, called from `OfflineRuntime`), and `collectStale()` only reaches an entry after `DefaultMaxAgeMs` = 30 days (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1138-1141).

So on the borrowed/shared machine this whole feature is scoped around, a session that expires (cookie dropped, backend restart, refresh failure) leaves the user's live entries — which are full gzipped `toBytes()` snapshots plus the change log — and their archives (whole documents) sitting in IndexedDB for up to a month. They are unreadable *through the app* by the next account (`listArchives`/`loadArchive` scope on `userId`, wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1028 and 1052), but they are plainly readable by anyone who opens DevTools → Application → IndexedDB on that profile. That is sensitive data at rest on a device the user no longer controls.

The code shows the intended middle ground was designed and then left unwired: `dropAllForUser(userId, { keepArchives })` exists (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1083-1123) and its comment at line 1116 says verbatim "`keepArchives` is for the one caller that did not ask for any of this: a session the server expired" — drop the live entries (copies the server still holds) while sparing the archives (the only copy of unsent work). `eraseOfflineData` plumbs the option through (offline-erase.ts:29). A repo-wide grep for `keepArchives` finds only those four sites: **no caller ever passes it**. The 401 path chose "erase nothing" instead of the option built for it.

Searched: grep for `keepArchives` across the repo (4 hits, all declarations); grep for `logout(` / `eraseLocalData` across `packages/frontend/src` (only `nav-user.tsx:41` calls `logout()` with defaults, and `api/auth.ts:256` with `"none"`); read `retryPendingOfflineErase`, `watchForOfflineDisable`, `collectStale` for any other expiry-triggered erase — none exists.

samples.summary: `collectStale()` deletes other accounts' live entries and archives without their authorization — including archives that are, by this feature's own design, the only copy of that account's unreconciled work
samples.evidence:
In `collectStale` the live-entry sweep walks `headerKeysWhere(BY_UPDATED_AT, range)` with no user scoping (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1167) and purges whatever it finds (1174-1185), and the archive sweep calls `dropArchivesWhere(BY_ARCHIVED_AT, range)` at line 1190 — again unscoped, even though `dropArchivesWhere` takes an `onlyUser` parameter that would narrow it (its signature and the `theirs` intersection are right there in the same file). `OfflineRuntime` runs this once per session for whoever is signed in (components/offline-runtime.tsx), so user A's ordinary page load destroys user B's data.

The file argues this is deliberate (lines 1144-1162) on the grounds that a departed account never returns to sweep its own. That reasoning covers *live* entries, which are copies the server still holds. It does not cover archives: the design states an archive is work the SDK could not reconcile — the only durable copy — and the same comment concedes elsewhere that `listArchives`/`loadArchive` refuse to hand one account another's precisely because an archive is a whole document. Deleting another principal's only copy of their data on a 30-day timer, from a session they did not authorise, crosses an account boundary in the destructive direction; the read side of that same boundary is enforced (line 1052) while the delete side is not.

Scope is local-disk only and age-gated, hence minor rather than major.

samples.summary: `dropArchive(id)` has no owner check, unlike its sibling `loadArchive(id)` which explicitly added one for exactly this reason
samples.evidence:
`loadArchive` refuses a foreign row — `if (!row || row.userId !== this.userId) return undefined;` (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1052) — and its doc comment (1041-1044) gives the reason: "an id can be held across a sign-out and the listing is not the only way in". `dropArchive` (1068-1073) takes the same caller-supplied numeric id and issues `tx.objectStore(ARCHIVES).delete(id)` with no `userId` comparison at all, so it will destroy another account's archive — a whole document, and that account's only copy of work the server never took.

Today's single caller is `recoverOfflineCopy` (lib/offline-copy-recovery.ts), which passes `work.id` obtained from `listRecoverableWork` → `store.listArchives()`, and that listing *is* user-scoped (line 1028), so I could not find a reachable cross-account delete. It is the guard that is missing rather than a live exploit: archive ids are a small monotonic auto-increment (the store is created with `autoIncrement: true`), so any future caller that derives an id from anything but the scoped listing silently gains cross-account delete. The asymmetry with `loadArchive` is what makes this worth closing.

Searched: grep `dropArchive(` across packages/frontend/src (declaration plus the one call in offline-copy-recovery.ts); read `listArchives`, `loadArchive`, `listRecoverableWork`, `recoverOfflineCopy` to confirm the only id source is scoped.

samples.summary: `documentIdsIn` swallows every listing failure and returns `[]`, so a deleted workspace or a revoked membership can complete while leaving full local copies of that workspace's documents on disk
samples.evidence:
`documentIdsIn(ref)` wraps `fetchWorkspace(ref).catch(() => undefined)` and `fetchDocuments()` in a `try { ... } catch { return []; }` (api/workspaces.ts, the new helper). `deleteWorkspace` and `removeMember` then call `purgeOfflineDocuments(doomed, { dropArchives: true })` with that empty list, and the server-side operation still succeeds — so the user is told the workspace is gone while every one of its documents, including archived whole-document snapshots, stays in IndexedDB on that device.

The same shape repeats one level down: `purgeOfflineDocuments` catches and only `console.warn`s (lib/offline-erase.ts:400-402), so a partial IndexedDB failure mid-loop leaves the remaining documents on disk with nothing reporting it.

This is the design's own stated rule — "content must not outlive the authority to read it" — failing open on the error path. The backstop is the once-per-session `purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments` reconcile in `OfflineRuntime`, which does catch this eventually, which is why it is minor rather than major. Worth noting that the reconcile is itself only reached under `PrivateRoute`, so a user who never signs in again on that device falls through to the 30-day sweep.

samples.summary: The path-traversal test's per-request assertion was weakened from "every URL carries the encoded id" to "at least one does"
samples.evidence:
The loop that previously asserted `expect(pathname).toContain(encodeURIComponent(TRAVERSAL))` for every request URL is replaced by a single `paths.some(...)` check. After the change, a regression in which one of several id-bearing requests stopped encoding its id would still pass as long as a different request in the same call encoded one.

The stronger half of the property survives — `expect(pathname).not.toContain('/auth/logout')` still runs over every URL, and WHATWG normalisation of a raw `../../auth/logout` would trip it — so I could not construct an actual traversal that now slips through, hence low confidence and minor severity. Flagging it because it is a deliberate loosening of a security regression test rather than of an ordinary one, and the stated motivation (a companion `fetchDocuments()` request with no id) could have been met by filtering to the id-bearing requests instead of dropping the universal assertion.

verdict.reason: Every load-bearing fact in the finding checks out against the repository. durable-session.ts:96-98 builds the Yorkie client key as `wb:${deviceSecret()}:${userId}:${docKey}`, and deviceSecret() (lines 137-154) reads/writes one global localStorage key, DEVICE_SECRET_KEY = "wafflebase-durable-device" (line 110), with no account component; I grepped all references and the only non-test callers are lines 139/144/160. Every account signing into that browser profile shares one secret, and the design doc agrees it is "minted once per browser profile" (offline-local-persistence.md:373). The permissive authorization model is also real: yorkie-auth.controller.ts:69 defines CLIENT_METHODS = {ActivateClient, DeactivateClient} and decide() returns ALLOW for them on token validity alone at lines 246-248 (mirrored at 292-296), with no document and no client-key ownership check — so the unguessability of the key is the entire control, exactly as the module's own comment (lines 80-94) states. I looked for a refuting guard and found none: no sign-out path clears the secret (offline-erase.ts:67-87 scrubs LAST_USER_KEY and per-user store content on a shared machine but never touches wafflebase-durable-device), and resetDeviceSecretForTest (line 157) is test-only. The only gate is a rollout pin — supportsClientKey() requires @yorkie-js/react >= 0.7.23 (yorkie-capabilities.ts:24,76-82) while package.json:66 pins 0.7.22 — but that is a feature-flag, not a security control, and the file itself says bumping the dependency is the only action needed to enable it, so it does not meet the already-guarded bar. Per-account scoping would genuinely mitigate the stated vector, since an attacker reading the profile before the victim first signs in could not pre-steal a secret minted at that victim's sign-in; and because sessions are cookie-based (offline-erase.ts:36-41), the device secret is exactly the artifact that outlives the attacker's window of local access, so it is not subsumed by ordinary shared-device risk. Exploitability's end state (DoS of the victim's durable session vs. client takeover) depends on Yorkie server semantics not determinable from this repo, which bears on severity rather than existence — consistent with the reviewer's major rating. In lane for the Security lens (secret scoping plus access control on client rows), and nothing here is concretely refutable.
